660.bp: Amazon and other marketplaces use a single featured storefront slot—the Buy Box—to show shoppers which seller to buy from. When Amazon removes the Buy Box, it's like turning off the lights on a seller's shop. Since 98% of sales flow through this single slot, losing it devastates a seller's visibility and sales.
660.wh: Amazon keeps the Buy Box hidden as a business decision, so outsiders don't know when or why it disappears. The researchers needed eight weeks of hour-by-hour tracking of 17,754 products to catch these hidden moments, and they had to coordinate data from 59,301 competing sellers at the same time. Most marketplace research can't operate at this frequency or scale.

The Buy Box isn't removed for just one reason. It could vanish because of competitor price changes, or because seller offers changed, or some mix of both. Separating these causes requires real-time data that didn't exist before.
660.ap: The researchers built their own data collection system to watch products hourly for eight weeks and open-sourced both the dataset and the code. For each product, they logged whether the Buy Box was present and what prices all competitors were charging. This let them see whether suppression happened right after a price change or competitor action.
660.ww: By watching suppression events happen in real time and comparing them to what changed just before, the researchers could see which triggers actually mattered. If suppression always followed one specific type of offer change, that change was likely the cause. Their real-time lens revealed that offer changes on Amazon itself were the main culprit, not rival prices.
660.po: The paper documents what happens when suppression hits: sellers lose search visibility instantly, ads disappear within 12 hours, and sales rankings drop 12% in two days. But the data also shows competitor prices don't shift—meaning the suppression isn't being used as a price discipline tool. The work exposes a crucial governance mechanism in marketplaces that directly harms sellers but flew under the radar until now.

661.bp: People are increasingly trusting AI chatbots (LLMs) with sensitive questions and decisions in web apps. But attackers can trick these systems into ignoring their safety rules and generating harmful content—misinformation, illegal instructions, or hateful speech. Keeping these systems secure is becoming a matter of public trust.
661.wh: AI companies have built defenses by training models to refuse harmful requests. But an attacker's goal is to find ways around those defenses. Traditional tricks like disguise (role-playing as a character, hiding meaning in code) are becoming well-known and less effective. A new attack method that exploits an unexpected weakness could break through.

Safety defenses look at the full prompt and the full response to spot danger. But no one had tried scattering harmful content across space—meaning breaking the request into pieces spread far apart in the input, or spreading dangerous phrases throughout the output in ways that look disconnected.
661.ap: The researchers developed SpatialJB, which spreads harmful content fragments across space in the prompt or response so that traditional safety checkers miss the pattern. They also built SpatialD, a detector that looks at the spatial layout of model outputs to spot when fragments cluster back together into harmful content.
661.ww: Safety systems are trained to detect dangerous content when it's concentrated and obvious. If the same harmful idea is broken into pieces spread across a longer text, the detector might miss it because each piece alone looks innocuous. The system can't easily tell that scattered fragments form a dangerous message.
661.po: SpatialJB beats widely-used attacks by 7x (95% success on GPT-4 vs. ~13% for Base64 encoding). Current guardrails catch less than 12% of spatial attacks, showing the method slips past defenses. The paper also offers SpatialD, a counter-defense, and demonstrates the attack works across GPT, Qwen, and other commercial systems deployed in real web apps.

662.bp: Self-driving cars need to see everything around them to avoid crashes. A single car's camera and sensors can only see a limited distance and angle. If nearby vehicles could share what they see, every car would know about hazards beyond its own line of sight, like a truck hidden behind a building.
662.wh: When multiple cars share sensor data in real time, they create massive communication overhead. Each car sending its sensor feed to every other nearby car uses huge bandwidth and creates redundant copies of the same information. This delays processing and makes real-time decisions harder.

Even if cars could share data, they'd still struggle to understand the full scene because the perspective is fragmented. One car sees the front of a pedestrian, another sees the back. Merging these partial views into one accurate picture is hard without global information.
662.ap: Octopus uses roadside units (stationary computers at the road's edge) as a hub. Vehicles send their sensor data only to the nearby roadside unit, not to each other. The roadside unit processes all the data together, builds a global picture of what's happening, and sends refined results back to each vehicle.
662.ww: A central hub (roadside unit) is much more efficient than cars talking to each other. One stream from each car goes to one place, where it's combined once, instead of N cars each sending to N other cars. The global picture built at the hub gives each vehicle context about the whole scene, which they can use to refine their own understanding.
662.po: Octopus cuts communication by 5,514 times compared to existing methods while improving detection accuracy by 11.58% in precision and 12.74% in recall. Vehicles get better awareness of their surroundings faster because the roadside unit's global view acts as prior knowledge, helping each car fill gaps in what it can see directly.

663.bp: The web is drowning in unstructured text—research papers, business documents, social media. This text contains knowledge (who did what, which countries border which, what causes what), but computers can't easily reason over loose prose. If we could automatically turn unstructured text into structured knowledge graphs, we could enable search engines, reasoning systems, and AI tools to work much more precisely.
663.wh: Converting prose into structure is a bottleneck. Traditional approaches use hand-coded rules or require humans to label thousands of examples to train a model. Both are slow and expensive. New LLM-based methods promise to scale, but they hallucinate (invent facts), miss nuance, and struggle with consistency across documents.

The challenge isn't just finding entities and relationships. Real documents also have events (what happened when), spatial-temporal information (where and when), visual layouts (images, tables), and metadata (author, date). Stitching these together into a coherent graph while keeping information accurate is complex.
663.ap: This tutorial covers the full pipeline: entity and relation extraction (pulling structured facts from text), event extraction, spatio-temporal indexing, visual layout parsing, and metadata handling. It then discusses how to build knowledge graphs by combining all these pieces and curating them for quality. Finally, it explores hybrid approaches that use LLMs to assist humans in knowledge engineering rather than replacing them entirely.
663.ww: Each part of the pipeline builds on the previous one. Accurate entities allow relations to be placed correctly. Events need time-place context to make sense. Combining LLM speed with human oversight (rather than trusting LLMs alone) creates graphs that are both scalable and factually reliable. This layered approach trades off speed for accuracy.
663.po: The tutorial describes a paradigm shift: from purely supervised models (slow, require data) to LLM-assisted engineering (faster, more flexible). It lays out what's possible with current tools—semantic search, reasoning pipelines, grounded dialogue—and identifies open challenges: scaling beyond pilot projects, ensuring all facts are verifiable, and measuring quality when the ground truth is ambiguous.

664.bp: Recommending products to users is hard when you have millions of items. To help the recommendation system learn what users like, it needs examples of items they didn't like. Picking which items to use as "negative examples" affects both how fast the system learns and what kinds of mistakes it makes.
664.wh: If you only show the model easy negatives (unpopular items that users obviously dislike), it doesn't learn to distinguish between popular items. If you throw in hard negatives (other popular items the user didn't click on) too early, the model gets confused and fails during training. Finding the right difficulty level at the right training phase is a balancing act.

Existing methods only score negatives from a small random sample of all items, so they might miss important negative examples. They also apply the same strategy throughout training, even though the model's needs change as it learns.
664.ap: R2NS uses three phases. First, warm-start: train with easy (random) negatives to build basic capability. Second, global recall: search across all items to find hard negatives that the model specifically struggles with, not just the top-ranked ones. Third, curriculum re-ranking: gradually increase difficulty as training progresses, like a tutor making tests harder as students improve.
664.ww: A gradual difficulty ramp prevents the model from getting stuck early (when it can't handle hard negatives) while pushing it to improve later. Searching the whole item space for hard negatives means the model sees examples that matter—items it confuses with the user's true preference. Dynamically adjusting difficulty means the model always trains at its edge.
664.po: The three-phase approach improves sequential recommendation performance by providing better contrastive signals. By recalling negatives from the global item space instead of a small sample, the model learns to distinguish users' true preferences from genuinely competitive alternatives, not just randomly unpopular items.

665.bp: The web connects knowledge across text, images, video, and audio. Some entities (like "Apple") appear as text in one source and as a logo in images elsewhere. Linking these together—recognizing that they're the same thing—would create a richer, more connected web of knowledge. But entities look different depending on the format, so matching them across formats is hard.
665.wh: Most alignment methods merge all types of information into one combined representation, treating text and images the same. But text and images capture different aspects: text tells you what something is, images show what it looks like. Combining them too early can wash out important differences. Also, two entities might be similar in one modality (both are people) but very different in another (different faces in images), and the method needs to catch both kinds of clues.

Current methods extract global features (the overall character of an entity), but miss local details (specific parts that distinguish entities). Without fine-grained matching, similar-but-different entities (like two people with the same name) get confused.
665.ap: DMEA extracts both global features (the big picture) and local features (fine details) from each modality separately. Then it computes alignment scores in two ways: intra-modal (comparing global and local features of entity pairs within the same format, like image to image) and cross-modal (comparing text to image). Each score is an independent decision, and the final judgment integrates all of them.
665.ww: Looking at local features catches details that global features miss—specific faces, unique textual markers. Scoring within-modality and across-modality separately respects that each format provides different evidence. Combining all the scores (not averaging them naively) means a high intra-modal text score and a high cross-modal score together make a stronger case than either alone.
665.po: By aligning entities at multiple levels of detail and across modalities, DMEA improves the accuracy of matching equivalent entities across heterogeneous knowledge graphs. This creates a unified web knowledge base where the same entity is correctly identified regardless of whether it appears as text, an image, or both.

666.bp: AI systems can have blind spots—they might work worse for some people than others (e.g., a face-recognition system more accurate on light skin than dark skin). Before deploying a model to real users, companies need to audit whether these fairness problems exist. Currently, auditing happens after training finishes, meaning thousands of wasted training runs before finding a fair model.
666.wh: Fairness depends on complex interactions during training that are hard to predict upfront. A model's bias against a group might emerge gradually or suddenly. Without training a model all the way to completion, it's unclear whether it will have fairness issues. This forces companies to complete many full training runs just to find which ones are fair.

Early prediction seems impossible because fairness isn't determined by initial settings alone; it emerges from the learning process. But if fairness trajectories follow predictable patterns, we might catch problems early without waiting for completion.
666.ap: The researchers tracked fairness metrics throughout training on multiple datasets. They looked at how fairness values changed from the start to the end and found consistent patterns: early-stage fairness strongly predicts final fairness. This means auditors can check fairness partway through training and make a go/no-go decision.
666.ww: If fairness develops monotonically (consistently improves or worsens), then checking at 10% of training gives signal about the final state. The paper found fairness trajectories are indeed predictable, meaning the learning dynamics that create fairness are stable enough to forecast.
666.po: By checking fairness during training instead of after, developers can stop unfair models early, saving 73.8% of training time in audit workflows. This shifts fairness assurance from a post-hoc expensive gate to an early-stage filter, making it practical to catch and prevent bias before deployment.

667.bp: Customer service teams spend time handling routine questions (password resets, order tracking, policy questions). Automating these tasks would free humans for complex issues. But current automation requires either hand-building rules for each scenario (slow, rigid) or training task-specific AI systems (expensive data collection, privacy risks).
667.wh: Most automation either relies on lengthy orchestration rules (a person has to code every step) or requires collecting and labeling lots of real customer conversations for each task. Both approaches are inflexible and slow. A system that learns from a generic description of a task would be faster, but LLMs without clear constraints often go off-track.

Data scarcity is also a problem: companies don't have labeled examples of every service task they want to automate. Privacy concerns mean collecting real customer conversations is risky. Deploying large LLMs in the cloud exposes customer data.
667.ap: The researchers define Task-Oriented Flowcharts (TOFs)—a diagram format that captures the steps and branching logic of a service task, like a flowchart. They build an algorithm that can extract this flowchart from a few example service conversations. Small language models deployed locally use the flowchart as a guide to handle new customer requests, avoiding the need to orchestrate rules manually or send data to the cloud.
667.ww: A flowchart is both expressive and constrained: it captures how service should flow without being so loose that the AI gets confused. Local deployment of small models avoids privacy leaks. Learning from few examples by distilling larger models (teaching smaller ones) makes the approach scalable without massive labeled datasets.
667.po: The framework automates customer service tasks end-to-end without manual intervention or cloud deployment. It outperforms hand-crafted baselines and commercial products on quantitative metrics, while preserving privacy by keeping customer data local and using smaller models that are easier to audit.

668.bp: Online, people debate claims about current events, politics, and policies. These debates contain both true and false statements, and understanding the arguments and disagreements is crucial for fact-checkers, journalists, and citizens trying to understand contested topics. But analyzing millions of online debates manually is impossible.
668.wh: Online discourse is messy: people use sarcasm, make opposing claims, cite each other, and shift topics mid-discussion. Extracting structured arguments from this chaos—identifying who claimed what and who disagreed—requires both computational precision and the contextual judgment that social scientists bring. Neither NLP alone nor computational methods alone can fully handle this.

Current NLP methods can extract entities or detect stance, but they miss the deeper conceptual foundations of why people disagree. A claim is true or false within a specific context, and understanding that context needs domain knowledge from political science, communication, and journalism.
668.ap: This workshop brings together researchers from computer science, social sciences, political science, and journalism. It covers NLP methods for finding arguments in text, detecting stance (does a speaker agree or disagree), and verifying facts. But it does this through the lens of communication studies and political science, grounding computational techniques in how arguments actually work.
668.ww: Bridging disciplines means the computational methods get reality-checked against what experts know about how debates work. Social scientists help identify what matters in an argument that pure NLP might miss. At the same time, computational methods help scale analysis beyond what manual review could do.
668.po: The workshop advances tools for analyzing online debates at scale while respecting the conceptual depth needed to understand contentious issues. Combining NLP (argument mining, stance detection, fact verification) with communication studies creates systems better suited to tracking misinformation, bias, and echo chambers in the wild.

669.bp: Social media bots—fake accounts run by algorithms—spread false information, amplify outrage, and manipulate public opinion. Detecting them is essential for protecting social networks from coordinated attacks. But as bots get better at mimicking humans, traditional methods (checking if an account posts at weird hours, for example) stop working.
669.wh: Bots don't act alone; they work together, coordinating with other bots and real accounts to amplify messages. A single bot might look human, but a group of bots working together shows patterns (like liking the same posts in the same order). Finding these patterns requires looking at relationships between many accounts at once, not just one account's behavior in isolation.

Most graph-based detectors look only at pairwise connections (who follows whom). They miss higher-order patterns—like when 10 bots all reply to the same post in sequence, which is a group pattern, not a pair. Traditional approaches also treat all types of relationships the same way (follows, replies, retweets) when actually the mixture matters.
669.ap: MPS-Bot uses simplexes—geometric objects that capture group structure—to represent higher-order relationships (groups of 3+ accounts acting together). It also uses attention mechanisms to learn how much weight to give each type of relationship (follows vs. replies vs. retweets) based on what's important for each user.
669.ww: Higher-order structure exposes coordination: bots don't just have individual properties, they exhibit synchronized behavior with other bots in groups. Weighting relationships differently for each user respects that some users are primarily followers while others primarily interact. This fine-grained representation is harder to spoof than simple features.
669.po: MPS-Bot outperforms existing baselines on two major Twitter bot-detection benchmarks (MGTAB and TwiBot-22). By looking at group patterns instead of just pairs, and by learning which relationships matter for each account, it catches bots that mimic human behavior and slip past simpler detectors.

670.bp: Large companies need to forecast their electricity use to manage power consumption efficiently and negotiate energy contracts. A company's power bill is also a signal of its financial health: unusual power spikes can indicate problems (inefficient operations) or opportunities (growth). Combining power forecasting with credit risk assessment—looking at both together—could give a fuller picture of enterprise health.
670.wh: Power consumption changes have causes: a company produces more goods, runs more servers, or shuts down an unprofitable division. These production changes affect both power use and the company's creditworthiness. But existing methods treat power and credit separately, missing the feedback loop: a credit downgrade (harder to get loans) forces cutbacks that reduce power consumption, and production failures (high power but low revenue) signal credit risk.

Most multi-task learning approaches share parameters between tasks or use simple attention, which doesn't capture the deep coupling. Power and credit data live on different time scales and structural patterns, and forcing them into one shape loses information.
670.ap: CPDGL is a multi-task system that simultaneously predicts power consumption and credit risk, but with explicit modules that model co-evolution. A path-interaction module directly captures how credit changes influence power strategy and vice versa. The system uses dynamic graph learning to model how relationships between variables shift over time.
670.ww: Modeling the feedback loop explicitly means the system learns that credit deterioration leads to power reduction, and unexpected power anomalies signal credit trouble. Using dynamic graphs instead of static ones respects that company circumstances change week to week. Handling different time scales and network structures separately preserves the natural patterns in each domain.
670.po: By modeling credit and power together, CPDGL improves both forecasting and risk assessment. Power anomalies become early warnings for credit problems, and credit trajectories help predict consumption patterns. The unified view gives energy managers and financial institutions better tools to plan and assess enterprise stability.

671.bp: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems let AI retrieve factual information from documents before answering, reducing hallucinations and allowing users to verify answers. These systems are increasingly used in education to help students learn. But if students can't see where an answer came from or how the system arrived at it, they lose the chance to think critically about the information.
671.wh: Transparency (showing which source a fact came from, what reasoning was used) is often treated as optional—a nice feature to add after the system works. But when students use AI to learn, hidden reasoning can actually harm learning: a student might memorize an answer without understanding why it's correct, or trust an answer without checking if it's accurate.

Transparency requires rethinking the whole system design, not just adding labels at the end. What information should be shown? When should it be shown? How do you balance helping users with respecting their independence?
671.ap: SAGE-RAI is a multi-purpose RAG system deployed in an educational context. It combines retrieval with an explicit focus on transparency: showing which documents the system pulled from, displaying reasoning steps, and explaining trade-offs. The researchers evaluated it through both numerical surveys (26 users) and deep interviews (4 users) to understand both satisfaction and learning outcomes.
671.ww: Making transparency architectural (built in from the start) means every design choice reflects it. The system can highlight retrieved passages and explain why they're relevant, letting users verify each step. This dual nature—serving both ethics (transparency as accountability) and pedagogy (transparency as learning support)—makes the investment worthwhile.
671.po: SAGE-RAI achieved 92.3% of users rating it 4-5 stars and high satisfaction overall (mean 4.62/5). The findings reveal that transparency serves both ethical and learning purposes: users could track reasoning and verify facts, but the study also identified tensions (students might over-rely on AI assistance). The work establishes that transparency must be foundational, not optional, in educational RAG systems.

672.bp: Taxonomies—hierarchical organizations of concepts—are everywhere: e-commerce categories, scientific classifications, database schemas. When new products or concepts emerge, taxonomies need to be updated. Manual expansion is slow and expensive. Automating this expansion would let taxonomies evolve with the world.
672.wh: Taxonomies have asymmetric relationships: "dog" is a type of "animal", but "animal" is not a type of "dog". Normal embedding methods treat relationships symmetrically (they care only about how similar two things are), so they struggle to capture asymmetric hierarchies. Trying to force symmetric methods into asymmetric problems leads to errors.

Existing approaches also don't capture ambiguity: a concept like "bat" (the animal and the sports equipment) has multiple meanings, and taxonomies need to place it correctly in different contexts. Box embeddings can capture hierarchy and disjointness, but they have technical problems: unstable training and no way to model uncertainty.
672.ap: TaxoBell replaces rigid point embeddings with Gaussian boxes—boxes centered and shaped by statistical distributions. A concept's location is its mean, and its uncertainty (ambiguity) is captured by its covariance (width). A concept is "inside" another concept if its box is contained in that box's space. Optimization is done using energy-based methods that are stable at boundaries.
672.ww: Gaussian distributions naturally encode both location (the hierarchy) and uncertainty (ambiguity). When you move a box, the energy-based optimizer is stable even at the boundary—no gradient explosions. The covariance handles polysemy: an ambiguous concept has a wider, fuzzier box, and the system can place it correctly even when it belongs in multiple places.
672.po: TaxoBell outperforms eight baselines by 19% in MRR and 25% in Recall@k on five benchmark datasets. By using Gaussian boxes, it handles ambiguous concepts better than point embeddings, learns more stably than previous box methods, and provides interpretable reasoning about hierarchical containment and uncertainty.

673.bp: Fact-checkers manually read documents and extract the central claims they want to verify. This manual process is the bottleneck: it's slow and requires expertise to know which claims are important enough to check. Automating claim extraction would let fact-checkers focus on verification instead of hunting for claims.
673.wh: What makes a claim "central" is a judgment call based on what human fact-checkers care about, not an objective property. Different experts might prioritize different dimensions: clarity, factuality, newsworthiness, sourcing. An automated system trained on generic examples won't capture what matters in practice.

Using large language models zero-shot (without training examples) is appealing but risky: they might extract verbose rambles instead of concise claims, or miss subtle claims because they're hunting for obvious ones. Without explicit guidance on what humans value, LLMs default to their own biases.
673.ap: The researchers first interviewed expert fact-checkers to extract what makes a good claim—call these Human Value Alignment (HVA) dimensions (clarity, relevance, supportedness, etc.). They then prompt large language models with these dimensions built in, telling them explicitly what humans value. For evaluation, they created an LLM-based scorer that rates extracted claims across the HVA dimensions and compares them to expert-written claims.
673.ww: By making human priorities explicit in the prompt, the LLM has guardrails: it knows to extract concise, supported, relevant claims, not just any factual statement. Scoring claims across multiple HVA dimensions means the evaluator can explain why a claim scores well or poorly, not just give a yes/no judgment.
673.po: The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on claim extraction (highest chrF and P@N scores). The HVA evaluator shows high agreement with human judgments and provides dimension-level breakdowns of claim quality, making it interpretable to fact-checkers. Zero-shot extraction now respects expert priorities without requiring labeled training data.

674.bp: Fact-checkers debunk false claims by writing counter-explanations. Some debunks come from professional journalists or established fact-checking organizations; others come from community members (like Twitter's Community Notes). Both types are important, but they might use different persuasion techniques. Understanding these differences could improve how fact-checkers communicate.
674.wh: The common assumption is that community fact-checkers, lacking training and editorial oversight, rely more heavily on emotional or persuasive language, while professionals stick to facts. This hypothesis hasn't been tested at scale: nobody has actually measured persuasion techniques across large datasets of both types.

Even if the hypothesis were true, it's not clear what to do about it. Are persuasive techniques bad? Do they help or hurt people's trust in the debunk? Community ratings might reveal whether rhetorical choices actually affect how useful people find the debunk.
674.ap: The researchers collected large datasets of Community Notes, professional fact-checks from EUvsDisinfo, and debunks from the Database of Known Fakes (DBKF). They quantified persuasion techniques used in each (emotional appeals, rhetorical questions, hedging language, etc.). They also examined how crowd ratings correlated with use of persuasive techniques.
674.ww: By measuring across diverse ecosystems and comparing ratings, the study can show both what techniques are used and whether they actually influence how helpful people find the debunk. Systematic rhetorical differences (if any exist) would reflect institutional norms and priorities, not just individual choices.
674.po: Contrary to the hypothesis, Community Notes don't use more persuasive techniques on average than professional fact-checks. Instead, the rhetorical differences reflect different institutional norms and topical coverage. Notably, the crowd effectively penalizes problematic rhetorical means when rating helpfulness, suggesting community self-regulation works. Notes with more persuasive elements receive slightly higher ratings, but only when the persuasion doesn't cross ethical lines.
